Krystle C. Kalafut 1,2, Yann Cormerais 1,2, Madi Y. Cissé1,2, Samuel C. Lapp1,2, Karen E. Inouye1, Gökhan S. Hotamışlıgil 1,3,4 & Brendan D. Manning 1,2

The nutrient-sensing mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) signaling pathway controls cellular and organismal growth and metabolism, and aberrant activation is linked to human disease, including metabolic disease. Cellular studies have established regulatory mechanisms inﬂuencing mTORC1 activation, but the physiological signals that control mTORC1 at the organismal and tissue levels are less well-deﬁned. mTORC1 is dynamically regulated by fasting and feeding in metabolic tissues, with both nutrients and insulin proposed to activate mTORC1 in response to feeding. Here, studies employing a liver-speciﬁc genetic mouse model demonstrate that AKTmediated TSC2 phosphorylation is the predominant mechanism of hepatic mTORC1 induction by insulin but is dispensable for activation by feeding. Furthermore, postprandial activation of hepatic mTORC1 requires dietary protein, which dictates the insulin-responsiveness of the pathway. Contrary to dogma, hepatic mTORC1 signaling was not elevated in response to dietinduced obesity, despite overt impairments in insulin and glucose homeostasis, and blocking hepatic AKT-TSC-mTORC1 signaling did not affect these metabolic phenotypes. Evidence is also provided supporting a role for glucagon in hepatic mTORC1 suppression during fasting. This study reveals a hierarchy of physiological signals regulating hepatic mTORC1.

The liver is a central hub for macronutrient metabolism that coordinates physiological responses to dynamic nutrient and energy states, such as across physiological fasting and feeding cycles1,2. To coordinate these metabolic responses, the liver must be able to both monitor and adapt to acute changes in nutrient availability. A key function of the liver is the regulation of glucose and lipid homeostasis in response to hormonal cues, such as those from insulin3,4. Importantly, hepatic insulin resistance is implicated in metabolic diseases, including obesity and type 2 diabetes5. However, the relevant targets of insulin signaling in the liver and the associated contribution to hepatic or systemic metabolism remain incompletely understood.

At the cellular level, mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) signaling controls the balance between anabolic and catabolic metabolism6,7. mTORC1 activation promotes anabolic processes and biosynthetic pathways in response to a variety of nutrients and signals propagated by growth factors and hormones, tailoring metabolism to local and systemic nutrient status6–8. In vitro studies have established insulin, as well as glucose and amino acids, as robust stimuli of mTORC1 activation9. In the liver, mTORC1 activation is sensitive to ﬂuctuations in nutrients, with acute activation upon feeding and suppression during fasting10,11, and aberrant hepatic mTORC1 activation has been linked to metabolic diseases4,12,13. Therefore, dissecting the mechanisms of hepatic mTORC1 regulation and its consequences for systemic metabolism is central to understanding metabolic control in health and disease. Insulin activates mTORC1 via PI3K-AKT signaling, and several mechanisms of AKT-dependent mTORC1 activation have been identi- ﬁed in cell culture models14–19. The most well-characterized mechanism involves AKT-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation of the TSC2 component of the TSC complex, a key regulatory hub that inhibits mTORC120–22. TSC2 is a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for the small GTPase Rheb, which facilitates maximal activation of the mTOR protein kinase by engaging mTORC1 at the lysosomal surface speciﬁcally when GTP-bound23–27. Therefore, the TSC complex inhibits mTORC1 activation by promoting the conversion of GTP- to GDP-bound Rheb. In response to insulin, AKT phosphorylates TSC2 at ﬁve distinct residues, corresponding to Ser939, Ser981, Ser1130, Ser1132, and Thr1462 of the full-length human TSC2 protein, and this regulation is required for full activation of mTORC1 in cell culture models20–22,26,28. AKTmediated phosphorylation of TSC2 inhibits the TSC complex by causing its dissociation from the lysosome, where a subpopulation of Rheb resides, thereby allowing Rheb-GTP to locally accumulate and activate mTORC126. The ﬁve AKT-mediated phosphorylation sites are conserved among vertebrate TSC2 orthologs, suggesting their physiological signiﬁcance in complex multicellular organisms, but this has not been directly tested in mammalian models22. The TSC complex is essential for the dynamic regulation of mTORC1 in the liver, as mice with liver-speciﬁc ablation of TSC complex components fail to suppress mTORC1 activation during fasting10,11,29,30. However, multiple signaling pathways converge on the TSC complex to either promote or suppress mTORC1 activity22, thus it is not entirely clear which signal is disrupted in such models. Like genetic loss of TSC complex components, other liver-speciﬁc mouse models used to study mTORC1 regulation in vivo, including genetic ablation of AKT or of mTORC1 components10,11,29,31–38, disrupt the entire, highly branched signaling network and may lead to compensatory rewiring not reﬂective of physiological signaling6,8. Thus, more precise models are needed to understand the physiological regulation of mTORC1 and its implications for health and disease. In addition to regulation by growth factors through the TSC complex and Rheb, mTORC1 activation is also sensitive to cellular amino acid levels through a pathway regulating a separate set of small G-proteins, the Rag GTPases, that control mTORC1 lysosomal localization39,40. In nutrient-replete conditions, Rag heterodimers consisting of RagA- or RagB-GTP (RagA/B-GTP) complexed with RagCor RagD-GDP (RagC/D-GDP) recruit mTORC1 to the lysosome, where it can access Rheb-GTP39,41. Insight from cell culture studies supports a model whereby maximal mTORC1 activation requires the presence of both extracellular growth signals and sufﬁcient intracellular nutrients to convert the Rheb and Rag GTPases, respectively, to the correct guanylate binding state to engage mTORC1 at the lysosomal surface40. Importantly, like liver-speciﬁc loss of the TSC complex, mice that express a GTP-bound mutant of RagA exhibit aberrant hepatic mTORC1 signaling even during fasting42, demonstrating that signals through both the TSC-Rheb and Rag pathways are critical for the proper dynamic regulation of mTORC1 with fasting and feeding. Given its role in metabolic regulation, hepatic mTORC1 signaling has been proposed to contribute to impaired glucose and lipid homeostasis in obesity and diabetes8,9,12,13,43. Some studies have concluded that hepatic mTORC1 is chronically elevated in obese mice, and mouse models characterized by repression of hepatic mTORC1 signaling exhibit protection from obesity-associated metabolic impairments4,12,13,38,44. However, the mechanisms driving hepatic mTORC1 activation in obesity and the causal link of hepatic mTORC1 to metabolic dysfunction have not been clearly deﬁned. It has been

widely proposed that chronically active mTORC1 can contribute to insulin resistance through negative feedback regulation of insulin signaling to AKT, with several distinct mechanisms described13,45–50. Furthermore, studies have shown that liver AKT activation in response to feeding or insulin is severely blunted in mice with chronic activation of hepatic mTORC1 and enhanced in mice lacking hepatic mTORC1 or its direct downstream substrate S6K14,10,12,29,51. Importantly, enhanced liver AKT activation in obese S6k1−/−12 or liver-speciﬁc S6K1 knockdown mice4 is accompanied by improved systemic insulin tolerance and insulin-mediated suppression of hepatic glucose production4,12. Thus, deﬁning the mechanisms underlying hepatic mTORC1 regulation by pathological signals, such as hyperinsulinemia and overnutrition, will be necessary to understand its putative role in metabolic diseases. Here, we describe a genetic mouse model that disconnects hepatic insulin signaling from mTORC1 activation. We utilize mice that conditionally express wild-type human TSC2 (TSC2-WT) or a TSC2 phospho-mutant that cannot be phosphorylated by AKT (TSC2-5A) in place of endogenous TSC2. Hepatic mTORC1 signaling is unresponsive to insulin but activated normally by feeding in liver-speciﬁc TSC2-5A (L-TSC2-5A). We ﬁnd that dietary protein is the dominant factor driving hepaticmTORC1 activation by feeding and that dietary protein content inﬂuences the role of insulin-AKT-TSC signaling in mTORC1 activation —a hierarchy that may be unique to the liver. In contrast to previous literature12,13, high-fat diet-induced obesity, hyperinsulinemia, and diabetes were not accompanied by elevated mTORC1 signaling in liver tissue. Furthermore, L-TSC2-5A mice were similar to L-TSC2-WT mice in the development of obesity-associated impairments in glucose homeostasis, despite mTORC1 signaling remaining unresponsive to insulin in this model. We also investigate glucagon as a negative regulator of hepatic mTORC1 and provide genetic evidence that glucagon signaling contributes to mTORC1 suppression during fasting. These data provide key insights into dietary inﬂuences on hepatic mTORC1 signaling and highlight the importance of understanding distinct mechanisms of nutrient-sensing across metabolic tissues.

Hepatic mTORC1 activation by insulin and glucose, but not feeding, requires AKT-mediated TSC2 phosphorylation AKT-mediated TSC2 phosphorylation is required for mTORC1 induction by insulin in cells26. To evaluate the role of this regulation in the intact liver, fasted L-TSC2-WT and L-TSC2-5A mice were treated with insulin or vehicle for 20 min, and AKT and mTORC1 signaling were assessed in liver tissue lysates. AKT was robustly activated by insulin in both L-TSC2-WT and -5A livers (Fig. 2a). This was also reﬂected in phosphorylation of TSC2 at T1462 in L-TSC2-WT, but not L-TSC2-5A, livers. Importantly, mTORC1 stimulation by insulin was impaired in L- TSC2-5A compared to L-TSC2-WT livers (Fig. 2a). As a control, signaling was also analyzed in gastrocnemius muscle from the same mice, where mTORC1 was stimulated by insulin to a similar extent in L-TSC2-WT and -5A mice (Fig. S2a), conﬁrming that the impaired mTORC1 induction in L-TSC2-5A mice is a liver-intrinsic effect. To determine whether L-TSC2-5A mice have deﬁcient hepatic mTORC1 induction in response to endogenous insulin secretion, fasted L-TSC2-WT and L-TSC2-5A male mice were administered glucose or vehicle via oral gavage and signaling was assessed in liver tissue collected after 25 min. Oral glucose administration resulted in signiﬁcant elevation in blood glucose and insulin compared to vehicle treatment, with similar levels in both L-TSC2-WT and -5A mice (Figure S2b, c). AKT was activated by glucose in both L-TSC2-WT and -5A livers, but the induction of mTORC1 signaling was blunted in L-TSC2-5A compared to L-TSC2-WT livers (Fig. 2b). It is worth noting that, despite this decrease in mTORC1 signaling in the L-TSC2-5A liver, AKT activation was enhanced in response to glucose, perhaps reﬂecting partial relief of mTORC1- dependent feedback inhibition of insulin signaling in the L-TSC2-5A livers. These results conﬁrm that TSC2 phosphorylation is necessary

for proper hepatic mTORC1 induction by both exogenous and endogenous insulin and suggest that insulin signaling through AKT and TSC2 is the primary mechanism by which glucose acutely stimulates hepatic mTORC1. The above experiments establish the L-TSC2-5A mouse model as a unique genetic setting in which to evaluate the contribution of insulin signaling to hepatic mTORC1 activation by a variety of physiological signals. To test its role in response to feeding, L-TSC2-WT and -5A mice were fasted or fasted and refed for 1 h. Plasma insulin was signiﬁcantly elevated in refed compared to fasted mice, with no differences between L-TSC2-WT and -5A mice (Fig. S2d). Somewhat surprisingly, mTORC1 signaling was induced by refeeding to a similar extent in both L-TSC2-WT and L-TSC2-5A livers (Fig. 2c). Since hepatic mTORC1 is disconnected from insulin regulation in L-TSC2-5A mice, these results indicate that insulin signaling is not essential for mTORC1 activation by feeding in the liver. The differential response of the L-TSC2-5A livers to glucose and refeeding was also evident by immunohistochemical staining of p-S6 in liver sections (Fig. 2d). Transcription Factor EB (TFEB) is directly phosphorylated by mTORC1 in a manner that issensitive to nutrients but isindependent of growth-factor-mediated regulation of the TSC complex and Rheb56–60. As expected, TFEB was phosphorylated in response to refeeding, but not insulin injection, similarly in L-TSC2-WT and -5A livers (Fig. S2e, f). These data also provide evidence that nutrient-sensitive mechanisms dictating mTORC1 recruitment to the lysosome, where it phosphorylates TFEB56,57,60, are intact in these mouse models. Given that TSC2 is also phosphorylated by AMPK, which is sensitive to energy and glucose levels, we evaluated whether differences in AMPK activation could contribute to hepatic mTORC1 regulation in L- TSC2-WT and -5A mice. Phosphorylation of AMPK and its downstream targets acetyl CoA carboxylase (ACC) and Raptor in liver lysates was unchanged in response to glucose or refeeding and was not different between L-TSC2-WT and -5A mice in any condition (Fig. S2g, h). These data are also consistent with previous ﬁndings that fasting is not suf- ﬁcient to activate AMPK in the liver30. TSC2 phosphorylation by AKT releases the TSC complex into the cytosol in cultured cells, while the TSC2-5A mutant is resistant to this spatial regulation downstream of insulin26,51. To test whether TSC complex release is similarly impaired in L-TSC2-5A liver tissue, TSC1 and TSC2 abundance in the soluble pool following permeabilization with digitonin of L-TSC2-WT and -5A liver tissue was examined. Both insulin treatment and refeeding induced cytosolic accumulation of TSC1 and TSC2 in L-TSC2-WT, but not -5A livers (Fig. S2i, j), suggesting that the inability of AKT to phosphorylate the TSC2-5A protein prevents the dynamic localization of the TSC complex in liver tissue. These experiments also suggest that phosphorylation-induced cytosolic localization of the TSC complex in response to refeeding does not underlie the induction of hepatic mTORC1 activation by feeding in L- TSC2-5A mice. The above results are consistent with fasting and refeeding studies in whole-body TSC2-WT and -5A mice, in which mTORC1 activation by feeding was retained in TSC2-5A livers, despite a clear defect in feeding-induced activation of mTORC1 in skeletal muscle52. Amino acids are necessary and sufﬁcient for near-complete hepatic mTORC1 activation Given that mTORC1 activation in cell culture models is dependent on amino acids8,40,61, we hypothesized that dietary protein content might override the insulin response in the activation of hepatic mTORC1 signaling by feeding. Indeed, quantitative metabolomics

revealed that plasma concentrations of nearly all amino acids were elevated upon two hours of feeding relative to fasted mice, with concentrations of alanine, glutamine, and valine being signiﬁcantly increased with feeding in this analysis (Fig. 3a (histidine not detected)). Plasma insulin was lower in response to the PF diet relative to the control diet, which likely reﬂects the established contribution of amino acids to pancreatic insulin secretion62–64. Furthermore, since insulin or AKT failed to compensate in its absence, dietary protein is the dominant signal contributing to the activation of hepatic mTORC1 by feeding. Relative to L-TSC2-WT livers, AKT activation was enhanced in the L-TSC2-5A livers under all conditions. However, mTORC1 signaling was only signiﬁcantly reduced in the CTL diet-induced L-TSC2-5A livers (Fig. 3c, see graphs for quantiﬁcation), a ﬁnding distinct from the response to chow diet-refeeding (Fig. 2c) and likely reﬂecting the difference in macronutrient content between these two diets (Fig. 3b; see below). To further determine the interaction between the insulin response and amino acid concentrations in the regulation of hepatic mTORC1 signaling, primary L-TSC2-WT and -5A hepatocytes were treated with a time course of insulin in the presence of high or low amino acids, while keeping all other media components constant. Insulin acutely stimulated AKT activation and TSC2 phosphorylation similarly in high and low amino acid media (Fig. 3d). However, basal mTORC1 signaling was greatly elevated in the high amino acid media, with only modest further induction by insulin (Figs. 3d and S3c). Along with lower basal mTORC1 activity, mTORC1 signaling was more overtly stimulated by insulin under low amino acids conditions in L-TSC2-WT hepatocytes, and this induction was almost entirely abolished in L- TSC2-5A hepatocytes (Fig. 3d). As an orthogonal approach to using more physiological levels of amino acids, the response to insulin was compared in L-TSC2-WT and -5A hepatocytes cultured in DMEM versus human plasma-like medium (HPLM)65, which has amino acid concentrations similar to that in fasted mouse plasma (Fig. 3a). As seen in the low amino acid media, insulin-stimulated mTORC1 signaling was impaired in L-TSC2-5A hepatocytes in HPLM (Fig. 3e). These results indicate that amino acid levels dictate basal hepatic mTORC1 activation and its dynamic sensitivity to insulin stimulation, with insulin signaling to mTORC1 being dependent on AKT-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2. Outside of transformed cells, such as HEK-293Ts, that have constitutive PI3K-AKT signaling, full activation of mTORC1 is thought to require signals from both nutrients and exogenous growth factors or hormones6. However, the results above suggest that dietary amino acids are dominant over insulin signaling for full activation of mTORC1 in the liver. To test this hierarchy further, L-TSC2-WT and -5A primary mouse hepatocytes were depleted of amino acids for one hour, followed by stimulation with amino acids and insulin alone or in combination. Amino acids were sufﬁcient to robustly activate mTORC1 in

both L-TSC2-WT and -5A hepatocytes, while insulin alone did not stimulate mTORC1 in either genotype (Fig. 3f). As expected, neither AKT activation nor TSC2 phosphorylation was induced by amino acids alone but was stimulated by insulin. The addition of insulin with amino acids modestly increased mTORC1 induction compared to amino acids alone, but this effect was not signiﬁcant. These results indicate that amino acids are both necessary and sufﬁcient for near-maximal mTORC1 activation in hepatocytes, providing an insulin-independent mechanism capable of activating hepatic mTORC1 in L-TSC2-5A mice upon feeding a normal chow diet.

Dietary carbohydrate-to-protein ratio governs the contribution of insulin-AKT-TSC2 signaling to hepatic mTORC1 activation The results above provide evidence that amino acid concentrations dictate the role of insulin signaling in the activation of hepatic mTORC1. Given the macronutrient differences between the CTL and chow diets (Fig. 3b), we sought to determine whether the dietary carbohydrate-to-protein ratio dictates the dominant route to mTORC1 activation in liver tissue by refeeding a high carbohydrate, low protein (HC-LP) diet. The formulated HC-LP diet derives 80% calories from carbohydrate and 10% from protein (Fig. 3b), as previous studies have demonstrated that short-term feeding of a 10% protein diet does not elicit markers of protein restriction66. Following one-hour refeeding with the HC-LP diet, hepatic mTORC1 signaling was induced by approximately seven-fold in L-TSC2-WT mice, with only modest and signiﬁcantly reduced induction in L-TSC-5A livers (Fig. 4a). Importantly, insulin levels in response to acute feeding were similar between the HC-LP (Fig. 4b) and chow diets (Fig. S2d). Thus, taken together with the primary hepatocyte experiments, these results demonstrate that lower dietary protein content renders AKT-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2 the primary route to feeding-induced hepatic mTORC1 signaling. While there are no known direct effects of mTORC1 signaling on hepatic or systemic glucose metabolism, mTORC1-mediated feedback mechanisms can, theoretically inﬂuence the insulin responsiveness of a given tissue10,11,29,67–70. Interestingly, accompanying the decrease in mTORC1 stimulation, the induction of AKT activation was more pronounced in the L-TSC2-5A livers with HC-LP refeeding (Fig. 4a), despite insulin levels being equivalent to those in L-TSC2-WT mice (Fig. 4b). Measurements of direct targets of AKT, including PRAS40 and GSK3α/ β phosphorylation, further demonstrated pronounced AKT activation in the L-TSC2-5A livers(Fig. S4a), indicative of enhanced hepatic insulin sensitivity. While in vivo evidence of purported mTORC1-dependent feedback mechanisms inﬂuencing hepatic insulin signaling is limited, it is likely that several such mechanisms function in parallel. Discussion The liver coordinates systemic metabolism in response to physiological nutrient intake. The mTORC1 signaling network controls cellular metabolism and is sensitive to local and systemic nutrient status, with low pathway activation in the liver during fasting and acute induction in response to feeding. By mutating TSC2 at the ﬁve AKT-mediated phosphosites that are required for mTORC1 activation by insulin in

cells26,28,52, we generated the L-TSC2-5A mouse model as a genetic tool to deﬁne the speciﬁc contribution of insulin-AKT-TSC signaling to the physiological regulation of mTORC1 in the liver. However, these models do not provide insight into the relevant physiological inputs integrated to control mTORC1 activation in this setting. AKT1/2 knockout mice have demonstrated that AKT is required for hepatic mTORC1 activation in response to insulin34,36. The ﬁndings described here provide mechanistic insights into this liver-intrinsic mechanism, demonstrating that insulin activates mTORC1 through AKT-mediated phosphorylation of the ﬁve sites on TSC2. Indeed, fructose was found in an independent study to acutely suppress hepatic mTORC1 in mice88. Published studies suggest that the dynamic nature of mTORC1 signaling in insulin-responsive tissues, including the liver, is critical to whole-body metabolic homeostasis12,29,38. It has been

proposed that liver mTORC1 activation becomes elevated in obesity4,13,89 and contributes to hepatic insulin resistance, with in vitro studies implicating a variety of negative feedback mechanisms on insulin signaling13,45–47,49,50. However, the present study found no differences in hepatic mTORC1 activation between mice fed a high-fat versus a low-fat diet, despite overt impairments in glucose homeostasis and hyperinsulinemia. Interestingly, we did ﬁnd mTORC1 activation to be elevated in skeletal muscle tissue of diet-induced obese mice. One potential explanation for the discrepancy is that some previous studies utilized a chow diet to control for HFD12,13. Chow diets contain minimal sucrose and various whole food ingredients that semipuriﬁed diets do not, confounding the comparison between obese and lean mice in these studies. Interestingly, obesity in humans is associated with elevated levels of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs)90, which have been proposed to contribute to insulin resistance, at least in part, through liver and/or muscle mTORC1 activation90–92. Given our ﬁndings that dietary protein and amino acids are dominant for the activation of hepatic mTORC1, it is possible that a BCAA–mTORC1 axis drives metabolic impairments in obesity without the necessity of broad, persistent upregulation. Another possibility is that zonal regulation of hepatic mTORC1, which is not reﬂected in immunoblots of whole liver lysates, is impaired under conditions of obesity84,93,94. Our ﬁndings contradict the purported dogma that hepatic mTORC1 is chronically activated in obesity, emphasizing the need for further investigation into the causal role of mTORC1 in tissue insulin resistance and systemic metabolic dysfunction. In addition to investigating mechanisms of hepatic mTORC1 activation, we also evaluated glucagon, which inhibits mTORC1 in hepatocytes and perfused liver tissue71–73, as a potential mediator of hepatic mTORC1 suppression during fasting. We provide genetic evidence in support of hepatic mTORC1 regulation by glucagon in vivo. The mechanism of mTORC1 regulation by glucagon remains unclear but is dependent on the canonical glucagon receptor and appears to rely on cAMP signaling, as it is recapitulated by forskolin, and seems at least partly independent of the TSC complex72,74. Glucagon promotes amino acid catabolism in hepatocytes and liver tissue95, which may contribute to its inhibition of mTORC1. However, it is likely that several mechanisms contribute to mTORC1 suppression during fasting, including a decrease in stimulatory signals from circulating amino acids and insulin. The metabolic response to fasting, including upregulation of glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and ketogenesis, is impaired in L-Gcgr-KO mice96–99. Given that several of these processes are opposed by mTORC110,11,85, it is possible that aberrant mTORC1 signaling contributes to the impaired fasting response in L-Gcgr-KO mice, but this remains to be directly tested. Importantly, the regulation of glucagon secretion is defective in obese mice100, leading to diminished dynamic shifts in plasma ratios of glucagon to insulin, which could also contribute to aberrant mTORC1 regulation in metabolic disease. This study demonstrates that macronutrient composition inﬂuences hepatic mTORC1 activation, independent of insulin induction, which could have important implications for energy balance and metabolic health. Important follow-up studies include evaluating how dietary insights gleaned from this study can be translated into insights for human health. Interestingly, restriction of dietary protein or select amino acids is sufﬁcient to promote longevity and metabolic health101–104, and lifespan extension is maximal in mice fed a low protein, high carbohydrate diet105. There is some evidence that these beneﬁts of low protein diets are mediated by reduced mTORC1 signaling, including in the liver67,106. Additionally, not only total dietary protein content, but protein source has also been found to inﬂuence hepatic mTORC1 activation and metabolic dysfunction in rats107. Quantiﬁcation of plasma amino acids by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry The method used for quantifying the absolute concentrations of plasma amino acids in mice following feeding was adapted from a previously described protocol111. Blood was collected from the tail vein in EDTA tubes (Microvette® CB 300 EDTA K2E, Sarstedt) and centrifuged to separate plasma. Plasma was mixed at a 1:10 volume ratio with a −20 °C mixture of methanol:acetonitrile:water (40:40:20) and a stable isotope–labeled internal standard13c labeled yeast extract (Cambridge Isotope Laboratory, Andover, MA, ISO1). These internal standards, together with a library of external metabolite standards, enabled absolute quantiﬁcation across a wide dynamic range. The sample was vigorously vortexed and then centrifuged at 4 °C at 13,000×g for 10 min. 30 μl of the resulting supernatant was transferred to an HPLC vial, from which 5 μl was injected into the LC–MS system for analysis. Chromatographic separation was achieved using an XBridge BEH Amide XP Column (2.5 μm, 2.1 mm × 150 mm) with a guard column (2.5 μm, 2.1 mm × 5 mm) (Waters). The mobile phase consisted of water:acetonitrile 95:5 for mobile phase A and water:acetonitrile 20:80 for mobile phase B, both containing 10 mM ammonium acetate and 10 mM ammonium hydroxide. The elution linear gradient was as follows: 0–3 min, 100% B; 3.2–6.2 min, 90% B; 6.5–10.5 min, 80% B; 10.7–13.5 min, 70% B; 13.7–16 min, 45% B; and 16.5–22 min, 100% B, with a ﬂow rate of 0.3 ml/min. The autosampler temperature was maintained at 4 °C, and the injection volume was 5 μl. Needle wash was performed between samples using methanol:acetonitrile:water. The mass spectrometer used was a Q Exactive HF (Thermo Fisher), which scanned from 70 to 1000m/z with switching polarity and a resolution of 120,000. Metabolite identiﬁcation was based on accurate mass and retention time, conﬁrmed against external standard pools, using El- MAVEN (Elucidata). Quantiﬁcation was performed either by stable isotope dilution, where a labeled internal standard was available, or by external calibration curves for metabolites lacking an internal standard. This approach enabled robust and sensitive quantiﬁcation of amino acids in plasma, resolving concentrations from low nanomolar to high millimolar levels.
